questions.question: A patient with exertional dyspnea has a heavily restricted calcific aortic valve. Carefully acquired echocardiography shows Vmax 4.4 m/s, mean gradient 46 mmHg and valve area 0.8 cm². LVEF is 58% and stroke-volume index 39 mL/m². Which classification best fits?
options: Severe high-gradient aortic stenosis
Moderate aortic stenosis with preserved ventricular function
Paradoxical low-flow low-gradient severe aortic stenosis
Classical low-flow low-gradient severe aortic stenosis
questions.explanation:
Concordant High-Gradient Aortic Stenosis

Correct answer: Severe high-gradient aortic stenosis

Hemodynamic Severity

**The measurements are concordant for severe high-gradient obstruction.** Velocity, mean gradient and valve area should be interpreted together rather than choosing one reassuring ventricular measurement.

The 2025 ESC/EACTS framework uses Vmax at least 4.0 m/s, mean gradient at least 40 mmHg and valve area at most 1.0 cm² for this concordant severe pattern.

Preserved EF describes ventricular systolic performance; it does not imply that the valve lesion is moderate or that symptoms can be ignored.

Clinical Assessment and Intervention

**Establish whether symptoms are attributable to the valve and assess intervention suitability.** Exertional dyspnea can also arise from lung disease, anemia, coronary disease or other cardiac abnormalities.

Confirm Doppler alignment, LVOT measurements, blood pressure and rhythm when findings conflict. This case is intentionally concordant and does not require a low-flow confirmation pathway.

A symptomatic severe lesion warrants prompt valve-team evaluation. The choice of surgical or transcatheter replacement depends on anatomy, age, life expectancy, procedural risk and lifetime valve planning. Preserved EF is not a reason to defer assessment until irreversible ventricular damage appears.

Moderate aortic stenosis with preserved ventricular function: Preserved EF does not downgrade concordant severe valve obstruction; moderate disease does not account for all three severe hemodynamic measurements supplied here.

Paradoxical low-flow low-gradient severe aortic stenosis: This phenotype has preserved EF but reduced indexed stroke volume and a mean gradient below 40 mmHg; neither the flow nor gradient in this case meets that pattern.

Classical low-flow low-gradient severe aortic stenosis: Classical low-flow low-gradient disease has reduced EF with low flow and a gradient below 40 mmHg; this patient instead has preserved EF and concordantly high velocity and gradient.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

questions.question: A patient with heart failure has a restricted calcific aortic valve, valve area 0.75 cm², mean gradient 28 mmHg, stroke-volume index 27 mL/m² and LVEF 32%. Measurements remain discordant after technical review. Which additional test most directly assesses whether the small valve area represents true severe rather than pseudo-severe obstruction?
options: Exercise treadmill ECG without valve imaging
Low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography
Repeat resting valve-area calculation after diuresis as the definitive severity test
Transesophageal leaflet planimetry as the sole determinant of severity
questions.explanation:
Classical Low-Flow Low-Gradient Aortic Stenosis

Correct answer: Low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography

Low-Flow Physiology

**Reduced forward flow can produce a deceptively low gradient across a severely obstructed valve.** Conversely, a poorly contracting ventricle may fail to open a moderately diseased valve fully, producing an apparently small area.

The reduced EF and low indexed stroke volume identify the classical low-flow phenotype. This is different from preserved-EF paradoxical low-flow disease.

Review LVOT size and velocity sampling, multiple Doppler windows, pressure and rhythm before attributing disagreement to complex valve physiology.

Dynamic Confirmation

**Low-dose dobutamine increases flow while valve area and gradient are remeasured.** A persistently restricted area with a rising severe gradient supports fixed severe obstruction; appreciable opening with flow favors pseudo-severe disease.

Inadequate flow augmentation can leave the test indeterminate. Projected valve area and CT valve calcium assessment can supply complementary information; lack of flow reserve is not synonymous with absence of severe stenosis.

Integrate the test with symptoms, valve morphology, myocardial disease and procedural suitability. True severe obstruction may warrant valve replacement, whereas pseudo-severe findings redirect attention toward ventricular therapy and surveillance. Do not select intervention from the resting valve area alone or deny assessment solely because the initial gradient is below the conventional severe boundary.

Exercise treadmill ECG without valve imaging: Exercise testing can clarify symptoms in selected apparently asymptomatic valve patients, but it does not provide the flow-dependent valve measurements needed to resolve this reduced-EF discordance.

Repeat resting valve-area calculation after diuresis as the definitive severity test: Optimization and repeat measurements can improve interpretation, but persistent discordance requires integrated testing; a small resting calculated area alone cannot reliably distinguish true from pseudo-severe obstruction.

Transesophageal leaflet planimetry as the sole determinant of severity: TEE can clarify valve morphology and selected anatomical measurements, but calcific shadowing and anatomical-versus-effective area differences limit a sole-planimetry decision; dynamic assessment directly addresses the low-flow question.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

questions.question: A patient with LVEF 30% has resting valve area 0.72 cm² and mean aortic gradient 25 mmHg. During technically satisfactory low-dose dobutamine testing, stroke volume increases by 28%, mean gradient reaches 44 mmHg and valve area remains 0.76 cm². Which interpretation is best?
options: Indeterminate stenosis because a stress gradient cannot establish severity
Pseudo-severe aortic stenosis with demonstrable flow reserve
True severe aortic stenosis without demonstrable flow reserve
True severe aortic stenosis with demonstrable flow reserve
questions.explanation:
True Severe Obstruction During Flow Augmentation

Correct answer: True severe aortic stenosis with demonstrable flow reserve

Valve Response to Increased Flow

**A fixed severely narrowed valve remains restricted as forward flow increases.** The rising gradient in this case unmasks obstruction that was underestimated by the resting gradient.

Pseudo-severe obstruction behaves differently: improved ventricular output allows greater leaflet opening and the calculated area increases beyond the severe range.

Review the area and gradient at each stage. A gradient increase alone, without the accompanying area and flow response, is less informative.

Flow Reserve and Treatment Assessment

**Flow reserve describes an increase in stroke volume, not merely a faster pulse or higher EF.** Here the 28% rise satisfies the conventional ≥20% definition.

A low-dose valve protocol differs from an ischemia-provocation stress study. EACVI/ASE guidance describes starting at 2.5–5 micrograms/kg/min and increasing every 3–5 minutes, generally up to 10–20 micrograms/kg/min, with appropriate monitoring and stopping criteria.

A symptomatic patient with confirmed severe obstruction needs valve-team assessment rather than medical treatment alone for the gradient. Conversely, lack of flow reserve in another patient would not automatically prove pseudo-severe disease or eliminate potential intervention benefit. Integrate myocardial disease, anatomy and procedural suitability with the valve assessment.

Indeterminate stenosis because a stress gradient cannot establish severity: Some dobutamine studies remain indeterminate, but adequate flow augmentation with this concordant small area and high gradient supplies a coherent true-severe pattern.

Pseudo-severe aortic stenosis with demonstrable flow reserve: Pseudo-severe disease shows greater valve opening with restored flow; the persistently small area and newly severe gradient support fixed severe obstruction instead.

True severe aortic stenosis without demonstrable flow reserve: The valve behavior supports severe stenosis, but the 28% stroke-volume increase exceeds the conventional 20% flow-reserve boundary.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

EACVI/ASE focused aortic stenosis echocardiography update, 2017 — https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/2017ValveStenosisGuideline.pdf

questions.question: A symptomatic patient with LVEF 28%, valve area 0.8 cm² and mean gradient 24 mmHg undergoes low-dose dobutamine testing. Stroke volume increases by only 6%; gradient reaches 27 mmHg and valve area is 0.82 cm². Which next approach is most appropriate?
options: Classify pseudo-severe disease from the failure to reach a 40-mmHg gradient
Use integrated assessment with CT aortic-valve calcium scoring to clarify severity
Classify true severe disease from the unchanged valve area alone
Calculate projected valve area and use it as the definitive result despite minimal flow change
questions.explanation:
Inconclusive Dobutamine Testing Without Flow Reserve

Correct answer: Use integrated assessment with CT aortic-valve calcium scoring to clarify severity

Recognize an Indeterminate Dynamic Test

**The absence of flow reserve is a limitation of the test, not a diagnosis of valve severity.** A 6% stroke-volume change does not meaningfully normalize the low-flow state.

Recheck acquisition quality and potential causes of limited response. Persistent myocardial dysfunction can coexist with either severe or less-than-severe valve disease.

Do not convert failure to reach a numerical gradient into proof that valve replacement cannot help.

Complementary Imaging and Projected Area

**CT valve calcium assessment provides information that is less dependent on the instantaneous forward flow.** Interpret sex-specific values with valve morphology and the clinical presentation.

Projected valve area estimates opening at a standardized transvalvular flow rate of 250 mL/s. It uses the relationship between area and flow during testing; it is not simply the resting area relabeled.

The 2025 ESC algorithm identifies projected area as useful with intermediate stroke-volume augmentation of 10–20%. Very limited augmentation makes extrapolation less dependable, favoring complementary imaging rather than forced classification. Calcium scoring also has limitations, particularly predominantly fibrotic disease and some bicuspid valves. The final decision combines symptoms, ventricular function, technical review and convergent valve evidence; no-flow-reserve status alone should not become a permanent refusal of intervention assessment.

Classify pseudo-severe disease from the failure to reach a 40-mmHg gradient: Without adequate flow augmentation, a persistently low gradient does not demonstrate that the valve would open normally at higher flow; the test has not established pseudo-severe disease.

Classify true severe disease from the unchanged valve area alone: An unchanged small area during minimal flow change remains ambiguous; the ventricle has not generated a sufficient dynamic challenge to distinguish fixed from flow-dependent restriction.

Calculate projected valve area and use it as the definitive result despite minimal flow change: Projected area can help with an adequate measurable flow response, but extrapolation from a tiny change is unstable and should not be treated as definitive in this study.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

EACVI/ASE focused aortic stenosis echocardiography update, 2017 — https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/2017ValveStenosisGuideline.pdf

questions.question: A hypertensive older patient with exertional dyspnea has a small concentrically remodeled LV, LVEF 62%, aortic valve area 0.8 cm², mean gradient 29 mmHg and stroke-volume index 28 mL/m². Which interpretation best guides further assessment?
options: Classical low-flow low-gradient stenosis from reduced systolic EF
Normal-flow low-gradient stenosis because EF exceeds fifty percent
A preserved-EF low-flow low-gradient phenotype requiring integrated severity confirmation
Concordant severe stenosis established by the calculated area
questions.explanation:
Paradoxical Low Flow Despite Preserved Ejection Fraction

Correct answer: A preserved-EF low-flow low-gradient phenotype requiring integrated severity confirmation

Ejection Fraction Versus Forward Flow

**A small ventricle can eject a normal fraction while delivering a low absolute stroke volume.** Concentric remodeling, impaired filling and reduced longitudinal performance can coexist with preserved EF.

Other contributors include atrial fibrillation, associated mitral disease or RV dysfunction. The low-flow label should describe measured forward output rather than be inferred from EF alone.

In the ESC 2025 framework, preserved-EF low-flow low-gradient AS has EF ≥50%, indexed stroke volume ≤35 mL/m², mean gradient <40 mmHg and area ≤1 cm².

Confirm the Lesion Before Selecting Intervention

**Review technical validity and control important loading abnormalities.** Check LVOT measurement, Doppler windows, rhythm and blood pressure; hypertension can complicate interpretation.

CT valve calcium scoring can provide complementary evidence when severity remains uncertain. Assess symptoms and alternative explanations such as HFpEF or pulmonary disease.

This phenotype is not proof that the valve is harmless, nor sufficient evidence for intervention from one calculated area. Integrate valve morphology, ventricular findings and convergent measurements. A symptomatic patient with confirmed severe obstruction should receive valve-team assessment; a less-than-severe lesion requires management of the actual cause of symptoms and appropriate surveillance.

Classical low-flow low-gradient stenosis from reduced systolic EF: Classical low-flow low-gradient disease has reduced EF; this case instead demonstrates the preserved-EF phenotype and requires assessment of its distinct contributors.

Normal-flow low-gradient stenosis because EF exceeds fifty percent: EF is the fraction of end-diastolic volume ejected, not indexed forward stroke volume; the measured 28 mL/m² establishes low flow despite preserved EF.

Concordant severe stenosis established by the calculated area: An area below 1 cm² raises concern, but the low gradient is discordant; measurement review, blood-pressure assessment and complementary evidence are needed before assigning confirmed severity.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

EACVI/ASE focused aortic stenosis echocardiography update, 2017 — https://www.asecho.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/2017ValveStenosisGuideline.pdf

questions.question: A woman has persistent discordant low-gradient aortic stenosis after expert echocardiographic review. Noncontrast CT gives an aortic-valve calcium score of 1850 Agatston units. Which interpretation is best supported by ESC 2025 guidance?
options: The score establishes high-gradient stenosis regardless of Doppler measurements
Severe stenosis is unlikely because the score is below two thousand
The score is indeterminate because a threshold above three thousand applies to both sexes
The calcium burden strongly supports severe stenosis using female thresholds
questions.explanation:
Sex-Specific CT Calcium Assessment in Discordant Stenosis

Correct answer: The calcium burden strongly supports severe stenosis using female thresholds

Use a Valve-Specific Calcium Score

**Noncontrast CT quantifies calcification of the aortic valve.** This is different from coronary calcium scoring and from contrast CT planning of an intervention.

Apply sex-specific thresholds. The same numerical calcium burden does not carry identical severity implications in men and women.

This woman’s score exceeds the highly specific female boundary, adding strong evidence to the integrated assessment without changing the measured hemodynamic phenotype.

Limits of Anatomical Confirmation

**Calcium supports severity but does not establish symptom attribution or the preferred procedure.** Assess the complete valve and ventricular findings and consider competing causes of dyspnea.

Predominantly fibrotic stenosis, some bicuspid valves and certain associated disorders can produce important obstruction without the expected calcium burden. A low score should therefore be interpreted with morphology rather than as an infallible exclusion.

Review acquisition and scoring quality. If evidence converges on severe symptomatic obstruction, proceed to valve-team assessment; if it remains inconsistent, resolve the uncertainty before selecting replacement. A calcium score does not itself supply a coronary anatomical assessment or settle transcatheter versus surgical suitability.

questions.question: A patient with a restricted aortic valve has LVEF 60%, stroke-volume index 42 mL/m², valve area 0.95 cm² and mean gradient 27 mmHg. There are no definite valve-related symptoms. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Paradoxical low-flow severe stenosis because the area is below one square centimeter
Normal-flow low-gradient discordance, often representing moderate disease, requiring integrated review
Concordant severe high-gradient stenosis because the area is below one square centimeter
Pseudo-severe stenosis conclusively demonstrated by the preserved EF
questions.explanation:
Normal-Flow Low-Gradient Discordance

Correct answer: Normal-flow low-gradient discordance, often representing moderate disease, requiring integrated review

Recognize the Discordant Phenotype

**The indexed stroke volume is normal while valve area and gradient disagree.** Do not force the case into a low-flow category merely because the area is small.

The ESC 2025 guideline notes that patients with this normal-flow low-gradient pattern usually have moderate stenosis. This is a population tendency, not proof in every individual.

Measurement error, body size, flow rate and the relationship between anatomical area and gradient can contribute to disagreement.

Resolve Uncertainty and Arrange Surveillance

**Review image acquisition and the clinical context before assigning severity.** Reassess LVOT dimensions, pulsed Doppler placement and the highest reliable transvalvular velocity from multiple windows.

Verify rhythm, blood pressure and whether the reported forward stroke volume is credible. CT calcium assessment or other targeted imaging can help when uncertainty is clinically consequential.

An asymptomatic discordant study does not justify automatic valve replacement from area alone. Follow the confirmed severity with clinical and echocardiographic surveillance, and reassess promptly if symptoms develop. Conversely, new convincing valve-related symptoms or convergent severe anatomical evidence should trigger renewed specialist evaluation rather than dismissal based on the usual moderate-disease association.

Paradoxical low-flow severe stenosis because the area is below one square centimeter: Paradoxical low flow requires reduced indexed stroke volume, which is absent here; the area boundary cannot replace the measured flow criterion.

Concordant severe high-gradient stenosis because the area is below one square centimeter: Concordant high-gradient severity requires a qualifying velocity/gradient pattern; the measured mean gradient is below the severe boundary and must be reconciled.

Pseudo-severe stenosis conclusively demonstrated by the preserved EF: Pseudo-severe disease is not established by EF; it describes flow-dependent restriction demonstrated through appropriate integrated or dynamic assessment, not a normal EF alone.

questions.question: A 74-year-old with confirmed severe high-gradient aortic stenosis develops exertional angina and near-syncope. LVEF is 61%. There is no major competing illness limiting expected survival or functional recovery. Which next management plan is best?
options: Prompt Heart Valve Team assessment for valve replacement
Optimize antianginal treatment and defer intervention until EF declines
Perform an exercise test before accepting the reported symptoms as an intervention trigger
Use balloon aortic valvotomy as the planned durable treatment
questions.explanation:
Symptomatic Severe Stenosis Despite Preserved EF

Correct answer: Prompt Heart Valve Team assessment for valve replacement

Indication for Intervention

**Symptoms attributable to confirmed severe aortic stenosis warrant valve replacement assessment even when EF is preserved.** Angina, exertional syncope or presyncope, and dyspnea are clinically important presentations.

Confirm symptom attribution and severity while assessing coronary disease, arrhythmia and other possible contributors. The stem provides an established severe high-gradient lesion rather than unresolved low-gradient discordance.

A normal EF does not measure all myocardial consequences of pressure overload and should not be used as a prerequisite for waiting until ventricular damage develops.

Selecting the Definitive Approach

**The valve team selects surgery or a transcatheter procedure through individualized assessment.** Consider valve and vascular anatomy, associated coronary or aortic disease, frailty, life expectancy, procedural risk and patient preference.

Temporary improvement with diuresis or other supportive treatment does not establish resolution of the obstruction. Treat decompensation while coordinating definitive care rather than substituting indefinite medical observation.

Intervention should offer a reasonable prospect of survival or functional benefit; major irreversible comorbidity may change that balance. When appropriate, explain recovery, prosthesis implications, follow-up and lifetime reintervention considerations. The decision to intervene and the choice of procedure are related but distinct questions: this patient meets a clinical indication without the vignette supplying every fact needed to select TAVI or surgery.

Optimize antianginal treatment and defer intervention until EF declines: Medical treatment can address comorbidity and symptoms but does not relieve fixed severe obstruction; preserved EF does not remove the intervention indication in attributable symptomatic severe disease.

Perform an exercise test before accepting the reported symptoms as an intervention trigger: Exercise testing is useful for apparently asymptomatic patients; provoking symptoms in an already symptomatic severe lesion adds risk and is not required to validate this presentation.

Use balloon aortic valvotomy as the planned durable treatment: Balloon valvotomy can bridge selected unstable patients or specific urgent situations, but restenosis and limited durability make it unsuitable as the usual definitive plan when valve replacement is feasible.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

questions.question: An independently mobile patient with severe high-gradient aortic stenosis and LVEF 58% reports no symptoms, but has progressively curtailed daily activity. There is no contraindication to supervised testing. Which assessment best clarifies whether the patient is truly asymptomatic?
options: A supervised symptom-limited exercise test with ECG and blood-pressure monitoring
A pharmacological perfusion study as the principal test of symptom status
A low-dose dobutamine study to distinguish true severe from pseudo-severe stenosis
Resting CT valve calcium scoring to determine whether exertional symptoms are present
questions.explanation:
Exercise Assessment of Apparently Asymptomatic Severe Disease

Correct answer: A supervised symptom-limited exercise test with ECG and blood-pressure monitoring

Unmasking Symptoms

**Self-reported absence of symptoms can reflect avoidance of exertion.** A supervised exercise test can reveal dyspnea, angina, presyncope or impaired exercise tolerance that the patient does not encounter in a restricted routine.

Assess symptoms, achieved workload, ECG and blood-pressure response together. The ESC 2025 discussion identifies a blood-pressure fall exceeding 20 mmHg as hemodynamic intolerance.

Testing belongs in a suitable monitored environment with an experienced team and appropriate stopping criteria. It should not be transferred to a patient already known to have symptomatic severe stenosis.

Using the Result

**Symptoms elicited during appropriate exercise assessment change the apparent asymptomatic classification.** The result informs intervention discussion rather than serving as an isolated numerical pass/fail label.

If the patient remains genuinely asymptomatic, assess ventricular function, progression, biomarkers and suitability for an early-intervention strategy under current guidance. Preserved EF and a normal exercise response do not mean follow-up can cease.

For surveillance, educate the patient about new symptoms and arrange clinical and echocardiographic reassessment, commonly at least every six months for severe disease under ESC guidance. An earlier review is needed for new symptoms. Physical limitations that prevent useful exercise testing require another individualized assessment; inability to test is not evidence that the patient has normal exercise tolerance.

A pharmacological perfusion study as the principal test of symptom status: Perfusion testing can answer a coronary ischemia question in selected patients, but does not reproduce ordinary exertion to assess valve-related exercise symptoms and hemodynamic tolerance.

A low-dose dobutamine study to distinguish true severe from pseudo-severe stenosis: Dobutamine is valuable for selected discordant low-flow studies; this lesion is already concordant severe high-gradient disease, so the unresolved issue is actual exertional tolerance.

Resting CT valve calcium scoring to determine whether exertional symptoms are present: Calcium assessment can corroborate anatomical severity when measurements disagree, but cannot establish the patient’s functional symptom status during activity.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

questions.question: Which interpretation of the EARLY TAVR randomized trial is most accurate when discussing intervention with an asymptomatic older patient with severe aortic stenosis and preserved EF?
options: Early TAVR reduced the composite of death, stroke or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization compared with surveillance
Early TAVR established an isolated all-cause mortality benefit as its primary finding
The comparison established TAVR superiority over surgical valve replacement
The comparison established benefit of TAVR in moderate aortic stenosis with reduced EF
questions.explanation:
Interpreting EARLY TAVR Without Overstating Mortality Benefit

Correct answer: Early TAVR reduced the composite of death, stroke or unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization compared with surveillance

Population, Comparator and Endpoint

**EARLY TAVR randomized 901 patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis to early TAVR or clinical surveillance.** It addressed timing of intervention, not a direct comparison with surgery.

The primary composite occurred in 26.8% versus 45.3%, hazard ratio 0.50 with 95% confidence interval 0.40–0.63. Interpretation must retain the endpoint components.

Unplanned cardiovascular hospitalization occurred in 20.9% versus 41.7%; stroke in 4.2% versus 6.7%; death in 8.4% versus 9.2%. These component figures should not be presented as if each independently established the same statistical conclusion.

Clinical Application

**An early-intervention discussion should consider trial eligibility and lifetime treatment consequences.** Asymptomatic status, stenosis severity, ventricular function, anatomy and procedural suitability matter.

Clinical surveillance is active care with symptom education, repeat assessment and later intervention when indicated. It is not permanent refusal of replacement.

The findings support reconsidering timing in appropriate severe disease, while leaving procedure selection to individualized Heart Team assessment. They do not establish benefit in every younger patient, every anatomy or every less-than-severe lesion. Explain potential procedural harms and later prosthesis-related decisions alongside the composite benefit. A qualified discussion is more useful than converting a trial result into a universal instruction to implant immediately.

Early TAVR established an isolated all-cause mortality benefit as its primary finding: The primary endpoint was a composite. Death occurred in 8.4% versus 9.2%; the significant composite result cannot be relabeled as a demonstrated isolated mortality benefit.

The comparison established TAVR superiority over surgical valve replacement: The randomized comparator was clinical surveillance, not surgery; the trial does not directly determine which replacement approach is superior.

The comparison established benefit of TAVR in moderate aortic stenosis with reduced EF: This is a different disease-severity and ventricular-function question; EARLY TAVR studied asymptomatic severe disease rather than that moderate-AS population.

EARLY TAVR randomized trial, 2024 online/2025 print — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2405880

questions.question: A 62-year-old with symptomatic severe calcific aortic stenosis has low surgical risk and a long expected lifespan. Both surgery and transfemoral TAVI appear technically feasible. Under the 2025 ESC/EACTS framework, which planning approach is preferred?
options: Favor surgical replacement while discussing prosthesis choice and lifetime valve management
Favor TAVI because technical transfemoral feasibility settles the modality decision
Favor TAVI because a low operative-risk score identifies the strongest transcatheter indication
Defer the modality discussion until the patient reaches seventy years
questions.explanation:
Choosing Surgical Replacement in a Younger Low-Risk Patient

Correct answer: Favor surgical replacement while discussing prosthesis choice and lifetime valve management

Age, Risk and Lifetime Planning

**ESC 2025 favors SAVR for patients younger than seventy years when surgical risk is low.** The threshold belongs to the stated framework and is not an isolated universal age law.

A long expected lifespan raises questions about prosthesis durability, future valve-in-valve feasibility, coronary access and the consequences of later explantation.

Surgical replacement also permits individualized mechanical-versus-biological prosthesis selection; the patient must understand the implications of lifelong anticoagulation if a mechanical valve is chosen.

Shared Decision With the Heart Team

**Technical eligibility for both procedures does not make them interchangeable in every patient.** Review valve anatomy, coronary and aortic disease, frailty, access, anticipated recovery and preferences.

A different balance may favor TAVI in an older patient or one with increased operative risk. Associated disease requiring surgery can favor a combined surgical approach.

Discuss the tradeoffs without promising identical lifetime outcomes from short- or intermediate-term comparisons. A procedural-risk score is one input and does not capture every anatomical or long-term issue. Document why the selected strategy suits this patient and what later interventions may be possible. The symptomatic indication establishes the need for replacement assessment; it does not remove the need to select the appropriate procedure and prosthesis.

Favor TAVI because technical transfemoral feasibility settles the modality decision: Feasible access is necessary for transfemoral TAVI but does not settle age, durability, coronary access and lifetime reintervention concerns in a younger low-risk patient.

Favor TAVI because a low operative-risk score identifies the strongest transcatheter indication: Low-risk TAVI trials inform shared decisions, but a low operative-risk score alone does not override the named ESC preference for SAVR below seventy years when surgical risk is low.

Defer the modality discussion until the patient reaches seventy years: Age informs procedure selection rather than postponing treatment of symptomatic severe disease; delay leaves an established valve indication untreated without a compensating clinical reason.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

Choosing Surgical Replacement in a Younger Low-Risk Patient

Correct answer: A — Favor surgical replacement while discussing prosthesis choice and lifetime valve management

Age, Risk and Lifetime Planning

  • ESC 2025 favors SAVR for patients younger than seventy years when surgical risk is low. The threshold belongs to the stated framework and is not an isolated universal age law.
    • A long expected lifespan raises questions about prosthesis durability, future valve-in-valve feasibility, coronary access and the consequences of later explantation.
    • Surgical replacement also permits individualized mechanical-versus-biological prosthesis selection; the patient must understand the implications of lifelong anticoagulation if a mechanical valve is chosen.

Shared Decision With the Heart Team

  • Technical eligibility for both procedures does not make them interchangeable in every patient. Review valve anatomy, coronary and aortic disease, frailty, access, anticipated recovery and preferences.
    • A different balance may favor TAVI in an older patient or one with increased operative risk. Associated disease requiring surgery can favor a combined surgical approach.
    • Discuss the tradeoffs without promising identical lifetime outcomes from short- or intermediate-term comparisons. A procedural-risk score is one input and does not capture every anatomical or long-term issue. Document why the selected strategy suits this patient and what later interventions may be possible. The symptomatic indication establishes the need for replacement assessment; it does not remove the need to select the appropriate procedure and prosthesis.

Other Options

  • B — Favor TAVI because technical transfemoral feasibility settles the modality decision: Feasible access is necessary for transfemoral TAVI but does not settle age, durability, coronary access and lifetime reintervention concerns in a younger low-risk patient.
  • C — Favor TAVI because a low operative-risk score identifies the strongest transcatheter indication: Low-risk TAVI trials inform shared decisions, but a low operative-risk score alone does not override the named ESC preference for SAVR below seventy years when surgical risk is low.
  • D — Defer the modality discussion until the patient reaches seventy years: Age informs procedure selection rather than postponing treatment of symptomatic severe disease; delay leaves an established valve indication untreated without a compensating clinical reason.

questions.question: A patient has cardiogenic shock from confirmed severe calcific aortic stenosis. The valve team concludes that definitive replacement cannot be performed immediately, but remains feasible after stabilization. There is no important aortic regurgitation. How should balloon aortic valvotomy be considered?
options: As a mandatory preliminary procedure before subsequent TAVI
As definitive treatment if the immediate gradient and blood pressure improve
As a selected temporary bridge to definitive valve replacement
As a reason to defer replacement planning until severe symptoms recur
questions.explanation:
Balloon Valvotomy as a Selected Bridge

Correct answer: As a selected temporary bridge to definitive valve replacement

Bridging Indication

**Balloon valvotomy may provide temporary relief of obstruction in selected unstable patients.** ESC 2025 permits consideration as a bridge to SAVR or TAVI, including selected urgent high-risk noncardiac surgical situations.

Selection requires a valve team because urgent definitive replacement may be possible and preferable in some centers. The stem specifies that it cannot currently be performed.

An explicit destination and reassessment plan distinguish bridging care from an unintended permanent postponement.

Benefits, Limits and Procedural Risk

**Improved forward flow can create an opportunity for stabilization, but the calcific lesion remains.** Assess blood pressure, perfusion, congestion and renal function after treatment.

Potential complications include vascular injury, bleeding, stroke, tamponade and important new aortic regurgitation. Existing significant regurgitation can make balloon treatment especially problematic.

Continue multidisciplinary shock care and reassess suitability for replacement as the patient recovers. If severe irreversible comorbidity makes meaningful recovery unlikely, clarify goals and whether an intervention offers useful benefit. Balloon treatment is not disease-modifying medical therapy and should not be represented as equivalent in durability to a prosthetic replacement. Its value in this question is a carefully selected temporary step with a defined subsequent plan.

As a mandatory preliminary procedure before subsequent TAVI: Balloon treatment can help selected unstable patients, but it is not a required separate preliminary admission for every TAVI candidate; direct definitive treatment may be preferable when feasible.

As definitive treatment if the immediate gradient and blood pressure improve: Immediate improvement can be valuable, but recoil and restenosis limit durability in calcific adult disease; a successful bridge does not remove the planned definitive valve assessment.

As a reason to defer replacement planning until severe symptoms recur: Recurrent symptoms can indicate loss of the temporary benefit; delaying planning until deterioration forfeits the purpose of stabilizing the patient for definitive intervention.

questions.question: A patient with chronic native aortic regurgitation has vena contracta 0.75 cm, regurgitant volume 72 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction 56% and effective regurgitant orifice area 0.36 cm². Holodiastolic descending aortic flow reversal and LV enlargement are present. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Moderate regurgitation because the LV remains compensated
Concordant multiparametric evidence of severe chronic aortic regurgitation
Indeterminate severity until pressure half-time is measured
Severe regurgitation established solely by the visible color jet length
questions.explanation:
Integrated Assessment of Chronic Aortic Regurgitation

Correct answer: Concordant multiparametric evidence of severe chronic aortic regurgitation

Concordant Quantitative Evidence

**Chronic regurgitant severity should be graded using multiple complementary findings.** The measurements in this stem all lie in the severe range.

Confirm the valve mechanism, jet direction, acquisition quality and the consistency of volumetric calculations. Eccentric or multiple jets can limit individual methods.

Assess LV volumes and function and measure the aortic root and ascending aorta. The ventricular response and associated aortic disease influence management in addition to leak severity.

Limitations and Further Assessment

**Pressure half-time depends on ventricular compliance and aortic–ventricular pressure equalization.** A short value can support severe disease but should not override the full study.

When echo measurements conflict or windows are poor, CMR can quantify regurgitant flow and ventricular volumes. TEE can clarify leaflet abnormalities or unresolved mechanisms.

The immediate next management decision depends on symptoms, EF, indexed ventricular dimensions and aortic anatomy. Severe regurgitation is not synonymous with immediate surgery in every asymptomatic patient, but it requires structured specialist follow-up and timely intervention assessment. Acute severe regurgitation is a different physiological setting and may lack the LV enlargement expected with chronic volume loading.

Severe chronic native AR marker | Common guideline boundary

Vena contracta | >0.6 cm

Regurgitant volume | ≥60 mL/beat

Regurgitant fraction | ≥50%

Effective regurgitant orifice | ≥0.30 cm²

Descending aortic Doppler | Holodiastolic flow reversal supports severity

Moderate regurgitation because the LV remains compensated: Ventricular compensation describes the response to loading, not a reason to downgrade multiple concordant severe regurgitant measurements; LV size and EF additionally guide timing of intervention.

Indeterminate severity until pressure half-time is measured: Pressure half-time is a supportive, load-dependent parameter rather than a compulsory gatekeeper; the supplied independent quantitative and flow findings already converge.

Severe regurgitation established solely by the visible color jet length: Color jet appearance depends on settings, driving pressure and eccentricity; severity is supported here by the integrated measurements, not by an isolated visual length criterion.

questions.question: A patient with aortic-valve endocarditis abruptly develops pulmonary edema and hypotension. Echocardiography shows leaflet perforation, severe aortic regurgitation, premature mitral closure and a nondilated LV. Which management approach is most appropriate?
options: Use intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation as the preferred bridge
Treat the infection and defer surgery until chronic LV dilatation develops
Urgent surgical evaluation with concurrent stabilization and antimicrobial treatment
Initiate beta blockade as the principal treatment for the compensatory tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Acute Severe Regurgitation Without Ventricular Dilatation

Correct answer: Urgent surgical evaluation with concurrent stabilization and antimicrobial treatment

Acute Volume Loading

**An unadapted LV cannot accommodate a sudden large regurgitant volume without a marked pressure rise.** Pulmonary edema and low forward output can therefore occur with normal chamber dimensions.

Early aortic–ventricular pressure equalization may shorten the murmur and produce premature mitral closure. Absence of a wide pulse pressure or long diastolic murmur does not exclude a severe acute lesion.

Endocarditis-related destruction and acute aortic root disease are important causes. Define the mechanism promptly with TTE and TEE when needed.

Stabilization and Definitive Treatment

**Acute severe AR with hemodynamic compromise requires urgent surgical coordination.** Start appropriate infection treatment and obtain cultures without delaying resuscitation or necessary intervention.

Provide respiratory and circulatory support. Vasodilator afterload reduction can be useful if pressure permits; shock requires individualized vasoactive support. These are bridges, not repairs of a perforated leaflet.

Do not apply chronic asymptomatic LV-dimension thresholds to this emergency. Mechanical-support selection must account for the regurgitant lesion: increased aortic diastolic pressure or LV afterload can worsen physiology. Reassess perfusion and congestion continuously while the valve and endocarditis teams plan definitive care. A temporary clinical improvement does not remove the structural indication or justify waiting for completion of an antibiotic course.

Use intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation as the preferred bridge: Balloon inflation increases diastolic aortic pressure and can worsen important aortic regurgitation; it is not the appropriate default support strategy for this lesion.

Treat the infection and defer surgery until chronic LV dilatation develops: Acutely elevated filling pressure can cause collapse before the LV has time to dilate; waiting for chronic remodeling ignores the urgent hemodynamic indication.

Initiate beta blockade as the principal treatment for the compensatory tachycardia: Slowing the heart can lengthen diastolic regurgitant time and impair compensation in acute severe AR; the priority is urgent valve care and perfusion support, not reflex rate suppression.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

ACC/AHA valvular heart disease guideline, 2020 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000923

questions.question: An asymptomatic patient has confirmed severe chronic aortic regurgitation. LVEF has fallen to 48% without another cause; LV end-systolic diameter is 47 mm. Surgical risk is acceptable. Under ESC 2025 guidance, what is the appropriate plan?
options: Continue surveillance until exertional symptoms are documented
Continue surveillance until end-systolic diameter exceeds fifty millimeters
Refer for aortic valve surgery based on LV systolic dysfunction
Use vasodilator therapy and reassess after EF falls below thirty-five percent
questions.explanation:
Ventricular Dysfunction as a Surgical Trigger in Chronic AR

Correct answer: Refer for aortic valve surgery based on LV systolic dysfunction

Independent Intervention Triggers

**Severe AR can warrant surgery before symptoms appear when ventricular function or size crosses the applicable boundary.** EF 48% satisfies the ESC established systolic-dysfunction trigger.

Confirm severity, measurement quality and the absence of another dominant explanation for reduced EF. Serial change helps interpret borderline values but should not be used to disregard clear dysfunction.

Assess aortic root and ascending aortic dimensions because associated aortopathy can independently influence the operation.

Attribute Thresholds to Their Guideline

**ESC and ACC/AHA frameworks use different EF boundaries and recommendation categories.** Do not merge them into a single undated cutoff.

ESC 2025 identifies EF ≤50%, LVESD >50 mm or indexed LVESD >25 mm/m² as established asymptomatic severe-AR surgical triggers. Selected low-risk patients may be considered earlier using additional evidence of ventricular change.

The ACC/AHA 2020 framework uses EF ≤55% when no other cause explains dysfunction. A lower-risk earlier-surgery discussion is not the same recommendation as an established trigger. Explain the rationale for intervening before advanced remodeling, document the measurement framework and coordinate a valve-center review rather than waiting for a heart-failure drug threshold.

Framework for asymptomatic severe AR | LV criterion | Interpretation

ESC 2025 established triggers | EF ≤50%; or LVESD >50 mm; or LVESDi >25 mm/m² | Surgery recommended when appropriate

ESC 2025 selected low-risk earlier discussion | EF ≤55%; or LVESDi >22 mm/m²; or LVESVi >45 mL/m² | Earlier intervention considered in context; distinct from established triggers

ACC/AHA 2020 EF trigger | EF ≤55% without another cause | Guideline-specific systolic-dysfunction indication

Continue surveillance until exertional symptoms are documented: Symptoms are an important intervention trigger, but their absence does not negate established LV dysfunction from severe chronic regurgitation.

Continue surveillance until end-systolic diameter exceeds fifty millimeters: The dimension and EF triggers are alternatives; crossing the EF threshold already supports surgery even though the absolute diameter is below fifty millimeters.

Use vasodilator therapy and reassess after EF falls below thirty-five percent: Treat hypertension and other indications, but the HFrEF threshold of thirty-five percent is not the surgical threshold for severe AR; waiting risks less reversible ventricular injury.

questions.question: An asymptomatic small adult has severe chronic aortic regurgitation, LVEF 60%, LV end-systolic diameter 44 mm and body surface area 1.5 m². Measurements are reproducible and surgical risk is acceptable. Under ESC 2025 guidance, which interpretation is appropriate?
options: The indexed diameter remains below the established trigger because EF is normal
The ventricular size trigger is absent because absolute diameter is below fifty millimeters
The indexed end-systolic diameter exceeds the established surgical trigger
Only an earlier discretionary intervention discussion is supported by these dimensions
questions.explanation:
Indexed Ventricular Size in a Small Adult

Correct answer: The indexed end-systolic diameter exceeds the established surgical trigger

Index the Measurement Correctly

**LVESDi equals LV end-systolic diameter divided by body surface area.** Here, 44 mm ÷ 1.5 m² = ==29.3 mm/m²==.

The ESC 2025 established severe-AR trigger is LVESDi >25 mm/m². This patient crosses it despite LVESD below fifty millimeters and preserved EF.

Report the units and measurement method. Do not divide by height, confuse end-systolic with end-diastolic diameter, or substitute an indexed volume boundary.

Interpret Size With Clinical Evidence

**Body size matters when interpreting chronic volume-overload remodeling.** A single unindexed cutoff can delay recognition in a small adult.

Confirm severe regurgitation and reproducible ventricular measurement, evaluate exercise symptoms where appropriate, and review serial function and dimensions. CMR can clarify ventricular volumes or regurgitant severity when echo is uncertain.

Refer for valve-center surgical assessment with the full anatomical and clinical record. Indexing is not a replacement for assessing symptoms, EF, aortic disease and operative suitability. Likewise, an apparently reassuring symptom history does not negate an established ventricular criterion. Explain that the intention is to intervene before advanced, potentially less reversible myocardial dysfunction, rather than wait for an absolute diameter derived without regard to body size.

The indexed diameter remains below the established trigger because EF is normal: Indexed diameter and EF are independent measurements; preserved EF neither changes the calculation nor cancels the size-based intervention criterion.

The ventricular size trigger is absent because absolute diameter is below fifty millimeters: The absolute boundary is not the only criterion: indexing identifies important enlargement in small adults, whose ventricular dimensions can be clinically abnormal below fifty millimeters.

questions.question: A low-risk patient is scheduled for surgery for symptomatic severe aortic regurgitation. Cross-sectional imaging confirms a maximal ascending aortic diameter of 48 mm. Under ESC 2025 guidance, what should the surgical plan include?
options: Isolated valve surgery with aortic intervention deferred until fifty-five millimeters
Assessment for concomitant replacement of the enlarged ascending aorta
Isolated valve surgery with aortic replacement considered only if subsequent rapid growth occurs
Plan a root replacement instead of evaluating the tubular ascending segment
questions.explanation:
Addressing Aortic Disease During Valve Surgery

Correct answer: Assessment for concomitant replacement of the enlarged ascending aorta

Concomitant Aortic Assessment

**Valve disease and aortic disease require a combined anatomical plan.** The root and tubular ascending segment are different structures and should be measured and described separately.

ESC 2025 advises considering concomitant root or ascending replacement at maximal diameter ≥45 mm when a valve operation is indicated and predicted surgical risk is low.

This is not a universal isolated-aorta threshold. Etiology, genetic disease, growth, body size, family history and operative circumstances influence aortic decisions.

Repair, Replacement and Valve Preservation

**Choose the operation according to the mechanism and the involved aortic segment.** Root enlargement with suitable pliable cusps may allow valve-sparing root replacement at an experienced center.

Calcification, cusp destruction or an unlikely durable repair may favor valve replacement. A tubular ascending graft and an operation on the root are not interchangeable labels.

Review CT or CMR alongside echocardiographic valve assessment and discuss durability, prosthesis implications and reintervention. A successful isolated correction of regurgitation does not remove untreated aortic risk. Conversely, a forty-eight-millimeter ascending measurement does not by itself prove that every part of the root must be replaced. The clinical value of the threshold is to prompt an integrated surgical decision rather than two disconnected treatment plans.

Isolated valve surgery with aortic intervention deferred until fifty-five millimeters: An isolated aortopathy threshold should not be copied into a patient already undergoing valve surgery; concomitant replacement can be considered at a lower diameter with low predicted surgical risk.

Isolated valve surgery with aortic replacement considered only if subsequent rapid growth occurs: Rapid growth is an important aortopathy risk feature, but the opportunity for concomitant replacement at the specified size should be assessed during the already indicated operation rather than reserved solely for documented future growth.

Plan a root replacement instead of evaluating the tubular ascending segment: Root replacement is relevant to root pathology; a tubular ascending measurement does not establish root enlargement. The operation should address the demonstrated segment and valve mechanism.

questions.question: An asymptomatic patient with chronic moderate aortic regurgitation has repeated blood pressures around 164/86 mmHg, normal renal function and preserved LV systolic function. There is no current intervention indication. Which treatment principle is appropriate?
options: Treat the blood pressure and reduce echocardiographic surveillance if readings normalize
Treat hypertension with an appropriate agent such as an ACE inhibitor or dihydropyridine calcium antagonist and continue valve surveillance
Use vasodilator therapy principally to postpone valve surgery even if later ventricular criteria appear
Choose rate-slowing therapy primarily to reduce the duration of diastolic regurgitation
questions.explanation:
Treating Hypertension Without Replacing Valve Surveillance

Correct answer: Treat hypertension with an appropriate agent such as an ACE inhibitor or dihydropyridine calcium antagonist and continue valve surveillance

Treat the Coexisting Hemodynamic Load

**Hypertension adds to the LV load imposed by regurgitation.** An ACE inhibitor, ARB or dihydropyridine calcium antagonist can be selected according to the patient’s clinical context.

Titrate to blood-pressure response and tolerability. Assess renal function and potassium with renin–angiotensin inhibition and monitor edema or hypotension with vasodilating calcium antagonists.

For example, amlodipine commonly begins at 5 mg once daily and can be increased to 10 mg daily; frailty or hepatic disease can require more cautious initiation.

Keep Medical and Procedural Indications Distinct

**Blood-pressure control does not repair a structurally incompetent valve.** Continue assessment of symptoms, LV size and function and associated aortic disease.

Do not prescribe prophylactic vasodilation to a normotensive patient as a proven method of postponing surgery. If established intervention criteria later appear, symptomatic improvement on medicines should not obscure them.

Beta blockers are not a blanket lifelong prohibition in chronic AR: arrhythmia, ventricular dysfunction or associated aortic disease may create another indication. Their use should follow that actual clinical problem rather than an incorrect claim about shortening regurgitant exposure. Explain why treatment is being prescribed and arrange follow-up so improved pressure is not mistaken for resolution of the valve lesion.

Treat the blood pressure and reduce echocardiographic surveillance if readings normalize: Pressure control treats an added hemodynamic load but does not establish that the valve lesion has regressed; surveillance remains necessary even after hypertension improves.

Use vasodilator therapy principally to postpone valve surgery even if later ventricular criteria appear: A vasodilator is justified for hypertension, but is not a proven substitute for surgery once severe-AR intervention criteria develop; indication and follow-up must remain explicit.

Choose rate-slowing therapy primarily to reduce the duration of diastolic regurgitation: Rate slowing lengthens rather than shortens diastole. Beta blockers can treat separate indications, but this proposed AR-specific mechanism does not justify prioritizing them here.

questions.question: A patient has moderate native aortic stenosis by valve-area assessment and moderate aortic regurgitation. Exertional dyspnea is attributable to the valve lesion after evaluation. Vmax is 4.2 m/s and mean gradient 43 mmHg, with reliable measurements and no alternative high-output cause. Under ESC 2025 guidance, what is appropriate?
options: Attribute the gradient entirely to regurgitant flow and disregard it in management
Continue surveillance until either isolated valve lesion is independently graded severe
Refer for valve intervention assessment based on symptomatic mixed disease with a high-gradient burden
Use balloon valvotomy as the preferred treatment for the mixed lesion
questions.explanation:
Combined Burden of Mixed Aortic Valve Disease

Correct answer: Refer for valve intervention assessment based on symptomatic mixed disease with a high-gradient burden

Pressure and Volume Load Together

**Mixed aortic disease cannot be interpreted by considering each component in isolation.** Regurgitation increases forward systolic flow across the stenotic valve while also producing chronic volume loading.

Confirm acquisition quality, valve morphology, regurgitant severity and ventricular response. Anemia or another high-output state can complicate the interpretation and should be assessed.

The gradient describes the combined hemodynamic burden in this setting rather than serving as a pure anatomical measure of stenosis alone.

Guideline-Specific Intervention Threshold

**ESC 2025 recommends intervention in symptomatic mixed moderate AS and moderate AR when mean gradient is ≥40 mmHg or Vmax ≥4.0 m/s.** This patient meets both hemodynamic boundaries.

Confirm that symptoms are attributable and use Heart Team assessment to select the procedure. Valve anatomy, aortic dimensions and accompanying disease remain important.

For asymptomatic mixed disease, the guideline also identifies Vmax ≥4.0 m/s with EF <50% not explained by another cardiac disorder as an intervention setting. Do not extend a recommendation based on these defined findings to every minor mixed lesion. Continue symptom education and serial ventricular assessment when intervention criteria are absent; combined loading may progress or be underestimated if follow-up focuses only on the word moderate.

Attribute the gradient entirely to regurgitant flow and disregard it in management: AR increases systolic transvalvular flow and can raise gradients, but that is part of the combined burden; it does not make qualifying high gradients irrelevant in symptomatic mixed disease.

Continue surveillance until either isolated valve lesion is independently graded severe: The combination can impose important pressure and volume loading even when individual lesion grades are moderate; the named guideline provides a specific intervention pathway for this mixed presentation.

Use balloon valvotomy as the preferred treatment for the mixed lesion: Balloon treatment does not correct regurgitation and can worsen it; mixed stenosis and regurgitation requires a replacement-oriented valve-team assessment rather than that default strategy.

ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf194

questions.question: A patient with mitral obstruction has doming of the anterior leaflet, restricted posterior leaflet motion, commissural fusion and subvalvular thickening. Which mechanism best explains these findings?
options: Obstruction from a left atrial myxoma
Degenerative stenosis from mitral annular calcification
Rheumatic mitral stenosis
Congenital parachute mitral valve
questions.explanation:
Commissural Fusion Identifies the Rheumatic Mechanism

Correct answer: Rheumatic mitral stenosis

Valve and Subvalvular Morphology

**Rheumatic injury can thicken leaflets, fuse commissures and shorten or fuse chordae.** The resulting funnel-like opening produces diastolic inflow obstruction.

Commissural fusion is particularly important because balloon commissurotomy treats fused commissures. A small orifice caused by another mechanism does not imply the same response to balloon treatment.

Assess mobility, calcification, commissural anatomy, subvalvular involvement and associated regurgitation rather than relying on one descriptive sign.

Implications for Evaluation and Treatment

**Mechanism determines which severity measurements and interventions are appropriate.** In suitable rheumatic anatomy, planimetry and integrated hemodynamic assessment guide management.

Degenerative annular calcification can create acoustic shadowing and a different orifice geometry, making straightforward planimetry less reliable. Such patients need a tailored multimodality assessment.

For possible commissurotomy, assess symptoms, valve area, pulmonary pressure, regurgitation and left atrial thrombus before selecting treatment. Associated aortic or tricuspid disease and coronary surgical needs can favor a surgical approach. Finding rheumatic morphology does not by itself establish that every valve is balloon-suitable; severe calcification, significant MR or atrial thrombus can change the plan. The examination distinction is therefore both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Obstruction from a left atrial myxoma: A myxoma can intermittently obstruct inflow but is an intracavitary mass; it does not itself produce fused commissures and the described leaflet/subvalvular remodeling.

Degenerative stenosis from mitral annular calcification: Calcific degenerative obstruction typically arises from annular and basal leaflet disease without the characteristic commissural fusion; its procedural options differ from rheumatic commissural disease.

Congenital parachute mitral valve: A parachute valve has abnormal chordal insertion toward a single papillary muscle; that congenital apparatus differs from the acquired fused-commissure pattern here.

questions.question: A patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis has a reproducible planimetered valve area of 1.2 cm². Mean transmitral gradient is 4 mmHg at a sinus rate of 48/min, with low forward flow. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Severe measurement error established by the area–gradient disagreement
Mild stenosis because the mean gradient is below five millimeters of mercury
Clinically significant mitral stenosis with a gradient reduced by the low-flow slow-rate state
Mild anatomical disease with an overestimated gradient from bradycardia
questions.explanation:
A Low Resting Gradient Does Not Exclude Important Mitral Obstruction

Correct answer: Clinically significant mitral stenosis with a gradient reduced by the low-flow slow-rate state

Anatomical Area and Hemodynamic Consequences

**Mitral valve area and mean gradient answer related but different questions.** Planimetry estimates the orifice, while the gradient depends on flow and the time available for filling.

A valve area ≤1.5 cm² defines clinically significant rheumatic MS in the intervention framework; ACC/AHA staging describes this range as severe. Older echo grading schemes may reserve the term severe for area <1.0 cm², so identify the framework.

Tachycardia shortens diastole and commonly increases gradient. Bradycardia and low output can produce the opposite pattern even when the orifice remains important.

Resolve the Clinical Discrepancy

**Record heart rate and rhythm with the reported gradient.** Check acquisition, average suitable beats when rhythm is irregular, and integrate pulmonary pressure and chamber changes.

If symptoms and resting measurements disagree, supervised exercise echocardiography can assess functional capacity, gradient and pulmonary pressure responses in an appropriate patient.

Intervention decisions require symptoms, morphology, thromboembolic risk, hemodynamic consequences and procedural suitability. Do not use one resting gradient as a universal clearance for exercise, pregnancy or surgery. Equally, a small measured area should be verified before treatment is chosen. The task is to reconcile anatomy with the physiological conditions under which the measurement was obtained.

Severe measurement error established by the area–gradient disagreement: Discordance warrants technical review, but physiologic dependence on rate and flow can explain it without proving that the area measurement is wrong.

Mild stenosis because the mean gradient is below five millimeters of mercury: A low gradient can reflect reduced transmitral flow and prolonged diastolic filling time; it cannot independently overturn a technically valid small valve area.

Mild anatomical disease with an overestimated gradient from bradycardia: Bradycardia tends to prolong filling time and reduce rather than inflate the gradient at a given flow; this interpretation reverses the physiological effect and disregards the measured area.

questions.explanationHtml:
A Low Resting Gradient Does Not Exclude Important Mitral Obstruction

Correct answer: C — Clinically significant mitral stenosis with a gradient reduced by the low-flow slow-rate state

Anatomical Area and Hemodynamic Consequences

  • Mitral valve area and mean gradient answer related but different questions. Planimetry estimates the orifice, while the gradient depends on flow and the time available for filling.
    • A valve area ≤1.5 cm² defines clinically significant rheumatic MS in the intervention framework; ACC/AHA staging describes this range as severe. Older echo grading schemes may reserve the term severe for area <1.0 cm², so identify the framework.
    • Tachycardia shortens diastole and commonly increases gradient. Bradycardia and low output can produce the opposite pattern even when the orifice remains important.

Resolve the Clinical Discrepancy

  • Record heart rate and rhythm with the reported gradient. Check acquisition, average suitable beats when rhythm is irregular, and integrate pulmonary pressure and chamber changes.
    • If symptoms and resting measurements disagree, supervised exercise echocardiography can assess functional capacity, gradient and pulmonary pressure responses in an appropriate patient.
    • Intervention decisions require symptoms, morphology, thromboembolic risk, hemodynamic consequences and procedural suitability. Do not use one resting gradient as a universal clearance for exercise, pregnancy or surgery. Equally, a small measured area should be verified before treatment is chosen. The task is to reconcile anatomy with the physiological conditions under which the measurement was obtained.

Other Options

  • A — Severe measurement error established by the area–gradient disagreement: Discordance warrants technical review, but physiologic dependence on rate and flow can explain it without proving that the area measurement is wrong.
  • B — Mild stenosis because the mean gradient is below five millimeters of mercury: A low gradient can reflect reduced transmitral flow and prolonged diastolic filling time; it cannot independently overturn a technically valid small valve area.
  • D — Mild anatomical disease with an overestimated gradient from bradycardia: Bradycardia tends to prolong filling time and reduce rather than inflate the gradient at a given flow; this interpretation reverses the physiological effect and disregards the measured area.

References

  • ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline, 2025
  • ACC/AHA valvular heart disease guideline, 2020
  • EAE/ASE echocardiographic assessment of valve stenosis, 2009

questions.question: Immediately after balloon mitral commissurotomy, a pressure-half-time calculation suggests valve area 2.4 cm², but technically satisfactory planimetry gives 1.6 cm². The patient is stable. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Diagnose early restenosis because planimetry is smaller than the pressure-half-time estimate
Accept 2.4 cm² because Doppler-derived area is independent of chamber compliance
Integrate planimetry, gradient, regurgitation and the clinical response because pressure half-time is unreliable immediately after the procedure
Repeat balloon inflation to make planimetry equal the pressure-half-time result
questions.explanation:
Pressure Half-Time Immediately After Commissurotomy

Correct answer: Integrate planimetry, gradient, regurgitation and the clinical response because pressure half-time is unreliable immediately after the procedure

Principle and Assumptions

**The conventional relation is MVA in cm² = 220 ÷ pressure half-time in milliseconds.** It is empirical rather than a direct anatomical measurement.

Pressure half-time reflects decay of the atrial–ventricular pressure difference. Altered chamber compliance, significant AR and other loading conditions can change that decay independently of valve area.

Immediately after commissurotomy, abrupt hemodynamic changes can invalidate the usual relation. A mathematically correct calculation can therefore yield a misleading anatomical estimate.

Assess the Procedural Result

**Combine anatomical opening with hemodynamics and complications.** Review commissural separation, planimetered area, mean gradient at the recorded heart rate, new MR and clinical status.

Use appropriate 2D or 3D imaging and check the plane of the smallest orifice. Planimetry also has technical limitations and should not be accepted without image review.

Do not pursue an idealized target by repeat inflation without considering leaflet injury or regurgitation. Arrange follow-up to document the sustained result once loading conditions stabilize. The useful distinction is between a method-dependent immediate discrepancy and evidence of a genuinely inadequate or complicated procedure; treatment must follow the latter assessment rather than a single derived number.

Diagnose early restenosis because planimetry is smaller than the pressure-half-time estimate: Disagreement between two immediate postprocedural methods does not demonstrate recurrent fusion or restenosis; it requires assessment of each method’s assumptions and technical validity.

Accept 2.4 cm² because Doppler-derived area is independent of chamber compliance: The empirical pressure-half-time relation depends on atrial and ventricular compliance and pressure conditions, which can change abruptly after commissurotomy.

Repeat balloon inflation to make planimetry equal the pressure-half-time result: A numerical discrepancy alone is not an indication for further inflation; additional dilation can cause regurgitation or other injury and requires an integrated procedural assessment.

questions.question: A patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis has exertional dyspnea despite a resting valve area of 1.7 cm² and mean gradient 5 mmHg. Symptoms remain unexplained after basic evaluation. Which investigation most directly assesses the valve’s contribution during exertion?
options: Repeat pressure-half-time calculation at rest as the sole next assessment
Transesophageal three-dimensional planimetry at rest as the next functional test
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing without simultaneous valve hemodynamics
Exercise echocardiography measuring symptoms, transmitral gradient and pulmonary pressure
questions.explanation:
Exercise Hemodynamics When Resting Measurements Underestimate Symptoms

Correct answer: Exercise echocardiography measuring symptoms, transmitral gradient and pulmonary pressure

Reproduce the Physiological Challenge

**Exercise increases transmitral flow and heart rate, potentially exposing an important gradient not apparent at rest.** Assess symptoms and workload alongside Doppler and pulmonary-pressure responses.

Check baseline rhythm, rate and blood pressure and select a supervised protocol appropriate to functional capacity. Avoid attributing every exercise symptom to the valve without considering pulmonary disease, ischemia or deconditioning.

If noninvasive findings remain unclear, invasive exercise hemodynamics can provide targeted clarification in a specialist setting.

Interpret Thresholds in Their Clinical Framework

**ACC/AHA 2020 permits consideration of balloon commissurotomy in selected symptomatic rheumatic MS with area >1.5 cm² when exercise demonstrates significant obstruction.** The cited findings are mean mitral gradient >15 mmHg or pulmonary artery wedge pressure >25 mmHg.

These are not interchangeable with a resting gradient threshold or a universal indication for every elevated exercise pulmonary pressure. Anatomy, MR, atrial thrombus and procedural expertise still determine suitability.

The aim is to connect symptoms with demonstrable valve physiology. A positive assessment informs treatment discussion; it does not bypass morphological contraindications. Conversely, a genuinely reassuring valve response should prompt renewed investigation of alternative causes rather than an intervention based solely on the patient’s symptom report.

Repeat pressure-half-time calculation at rest as the sole next assessment: Repeat acquisition can resolve technical error, but a resting calculation alone does not reproduce the exercise-related hemodynamic question when the resting study is already adequate.

Transesophageal three-dimensional planimetry at rest as the next functional test: TEE can clarify uncertain orifice anatomy or thrombus, but a resting anatomical measurement does not directly reproduce the exertional gradient and symptoms in this adequately imaged patient.

Cardiopulmonary exercise testing without simultaneous valve hemodynamics: CPET can quantify limitation and suggest cardiac versus pulmonary contributors, but by itself does not measure the exercise transmitral gradient or pulmonary-pressure response needed to link symptoms to this lesion.

questions.question: A patient has persistent NYHA III symptoms from rheumatic mitral stenosis despite appropriate medical treatment. Valve area is 1.0 cm², with mobile leaflets, commissural fusion, limited calcification and only mild MR. TEE excludes LA thrombus. No other cardiac lesion requires surgery. Which intervention is preferred?
options: Open surgical commissurotomy as the initial procedure
Surgical mitral replacement as the initial procedure
Percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy at an experienced valve center
Continued medical therapy without a procedural plan
questions.explanation:
Selecting Balloon Commissurotomy for Favorable Rheumatic Anatomy

Correct answer: Percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy at an experienced valve center

Mechanism-Based Intervention

**Balloon commissurotomy separates fused commissures.** Its success depends on the mechanism and distribution of valve disease rather than valve area alone.

Review leaflet mobility, thickening, calcification and subvalvular disease. Anatomy scores support assessment, but do not replace direct review of commissures or associated MR.

A favorable total score cannot cancel a contraindication. Severe or bicommissural calcification and absent commissural fusion substantially change suitability.

Eligibility and Safety Assessment

**Confirm important stenosis, a clinical indication and absence of major exclusions.** TEE is used to exclude LA thrombus before the procedure.

More than mild MR is a contraindication in the ESC framework. Significant concomitant aortic or tricuspid disease requiring surgery, or coronary disease requiring bypass, can favor a surgical strategy.

Explain risks including important MR, embolism, tamponade and an inadequate result. Reassess valve opening, gradient at the documented heart rate, residual regurgitation and symptoms afterward. Medical treatment for rate or volume control may still be necessary. Commissurotomy is an intervention on the mechanical obstruction, not a substitute for thromboembolic prevention or follow-up for recurrent disease.

Open surgical commissurotomy as the initial procedure: Surgical commissurotomy can preserve the valve when catheter treatment is unsuitable or another operation is needed; favorable balloon anatomy without a surgical co-indication supports percutaneous treatment first.

Surgical mitral replacement as the initial procedure: Replacement is important when anatomy or associated disease makes commissurotomy unsuitable, but favorable commissural anatomy without a surgical co-indication supports the less invasive commissurotomy pathway here.

Continued medical therapy without a procedural plan: Diuresis and rate control may reduce symptoms but do not remove fused commissures; persistent substantial symptoms with clinically severe suitable rheumatic MS support intervention.
